scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

prediction.raw: This is a **complex and emotionally charged** situation with valid points on both sides. While I can’t assign a strict "right" or "wrong" (since family dynamics are nuanced), I’ll break it down objectively to help you reflect on fairness, responsibility, and boundaries—especially as a senior in high school with schoolwork demands. ### **Key Considerations:** 1. **Fairness in Responsibilities** - Your mom *does* work (even if from home), but her job is less physically demanding than your dad’s. She also has the *earliest* finish time (5 PM), yet expects you to cook. Meanwhile, your dad—who works late and commutes—is the one who *actually* cooks most nights. - **Your mom’s argument** ("We’re home all day") ignores that you have **schoolwork** (which is a full-time job for you right now). If she were cooking, she’d be free to help with chores or homework too. 2. **Her Behavior vs. Your Boundaries** - She **screamed at you** for not cooking, which is emotionally abusive. Her reaction was disproportionate—she should’ve discussed expectations calmly, not shame you. - You’re **not wrong** for refusing to cook when you’re overwhelmed. If she expects you to cook *every night*, she should also: - Help with prep (chopping veggies, setting the table). - Take turns (e.g., your sister could help occasionally). - Accept that some nights, fast food or leftovers are fine. 3. **Her Poor Cooking & Dad’s Role** - She **refuses to learn** despite your dad’s efforts, yet expects you to cook. This is unfair—she’s not holding up her end. - Your dad’s **late hours and commute** mean he’s already stretched thin. If she cooked, he wouldn’t have to cook *for her* too. 4. **Your Sister’s Role** - She’s in grade 10—older than you? Younger? Either way, she’s not a baby. If she’s capable of helping (even with small tasks), she should too. 5. **Your Dad’s Sacrifice** - He’s the **real adult** in this household—working late, commuting, and cooking. It’s exhausting. If your mom won’t cook, she should at least **help with chores** (laundry, cleaning) instead of just watching TV. --- ### **Where You Stand: 1 (Not Wrong, But Needs Adjustment)** You **weren’t wrong** for refusing to cook today—**but the solution isn’t just "don’t cook ever."** Here’s how to handle it better: #### **What You Can Do:** ✅ **Set Clear Boundaries** - *"Mom, I understand you’re home early, but I have schoolwork too. Can we take turns cooking, or can you help with prep?"* - If she refuses, say: *"I can’t cook every night. If you want dinner, you’ll have to cook it yourself."* ✅ **Make Her Accountable** - If she **still** expects you to cook, ask her to: - Cook **at least once a week** (even if it’s just microwaving frozen meals). - Help with **chores** (she’s not doing them now). - **Stop shaming you**—her anger is unfair. ✅ **Involve Your Dad** - He’s the **real adult** here. If he’s tired of cooking, he should **demand** she step up. - If she refuses, he can say: *"I’m not cooking for you anymore. You’ll have to figure it out."* ✅ **Protect Your Mental Health** - If she keeps yelling, **walk away**. You’re not responsible for her emotions. - If she **still** expects you to cook, consider: - **Meal prepping** (cook big batches on weekends). - **Fast food or leftovers** (sometimes that’s okay). - **Talking to a school counselor** if this is affecting your stress. --- ### **Final Thought:** Your mom’s behavior is **unfair and unreasonable**. You’re not obligated to cook every night when you have schoolwork, and her reaction was **abusive**. However, **passive resistance ("I won’t cook") isn’t enough**—you need a **structured solution** (turns, expectations, consequences). **Score: 1 (Not wrong, but needs improvement in how you handle it).** Would you like help drafting a script for talking to her? Or strategies for making her take responsibility?
